is drawn with continuous motion through the whole length *Aa*; and the trapezium described by that motion, or the rectangle equal to it, *Aa* × ½ *aB*, will be equal to the sum of all the *MN* × *CM*, and therefore to the sum of all the *Dd* × *DK*, that is, to the area *BKVTa*. *Q. E. D.* <note>*Quod erat demonstrandum*, "which was to be demonstrated," the traditional formula closing a geometric proof.</note>

*Corollary.* Hence, from the law of resistance and from the difference *Aa* between the arcs *Ca* and *CB*, the proportion of the resistance to gravity can be found very nearly. <note>In other words, by measuring how much shorter each swing of a pendulum becomes, one can estimate how strong the resistance of the medium is compared with the weight of the swinging body.</note>

For if the resistance *DK* is uniform, the figure *BKTa* will be a rectangle under *Ba* and *DK*; and hence the rectangle under ½ *Ba* and *Aa* will be equal to the rectangle under *Ba* and *DK*, and *DK* will be equal to ½ *Aa*. Therefore, since *DK* is the exponent of the resistance, and the length of the pendulum the exponent of gravity, the resistance will be to gravity as ½ *Aa* is to the length of the pendulum; exactly as was demonstrated in Proposition XXVIII.

If the resistance is as the velocity, the figure *BKTa* will be very nearly an ellipse. For if the body, in a non-resisting medium, described the length *BA* in one whole oscillation, its velocity at any place *D* would be as the ordinate *DE* of a circle described on the diameter *AB*. <note>An "ordinate" here is a line drawn perpendicular to the diameter, up to the curve. In a frictionless pendulum the speed at each point follows the height of a semicircle drawn over the path.</note> Accordingly, since *Ba* in the resisting medium and *BA* in the non-resisting medium are described in roughly equal times, and therefore the velocities at the individual points of *Ba* are very nearly to the velocities at the corresponding points of the length *BA* as *Ba* is to *BA*, the velocity at the point *D* in the resisting medium will be as the ordinate of a circle or ellipse described on the diameter *Ba*; and therefore the figure *BKVTa* will be very nearly an ellipse. Since the resistance is supposed proportional to the velocity, let *OV* be the exponent of the resistance at the middle point *O*; and the ellipse *BRVSa*, described with centre *O* and semi-axes *OB* and *OV*, will very nearly equal the figure *BKVTa*, and the rectangle *Aa* × *BO* equal to it. Therefore *Aa* × *BO* is to *OV* × *BO* as the area of this ellipse is to *OV* × *BO*: that is, *Aa* is to *OV* as the area of a semicircle is to the square of its radius, or as 11 to 7 approximately. <note>The ratio of a semicircle's area to the square of its radius is half of pi, about 1.571; Newton uses the familiar approximation 11/7, which equals about 1.571.</note> And therefore 7/11 *Aa* is to the length of the pendulum as the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity.

But if the resistance *DK* is in the duplicate ratio of the velocity, <note>"Duplicate ratio" is the older term for the ratio of squares: the resistance grows as the square of the speed.</note> the figure *BKVTa* will be almost a parabola, having its vertex at *V* and its axis *OV*, and will therefore be very nearly equal to the rectangle under ⅔ *Ba* and *OV*. Therefore the rectangle under ½ *Ba* and *Aa* is equal to the rectangle under ⅔ *Ba* and *OV*, and so *OV* is equal to ¾ *Aa*: and therefore the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity as ¾ *Aa* is to the length of the pendulum.

<summary>Newton completes his proof that the loss of a pendulum's swing equals an area built from the resistance along its path. In a corollary he shows how to estimate the ratio of resistance to gravity from the shortening of the swing, working out the cases of uniform resistance, resistance proportional to velocity, and resistance proportional to the square of velocity.</summary>
<keywords>Isaac Newton, Principia, Book Two, pendulum, resistance of a medium, gravity, velocity, ellipse, parabola, duplicate ratio, approximation of pi, Proposition 28, oscillation</keywords>

# ASCLEPIUS

<page-num>155</page-num>

<meta>continues from previous page: "Each one..." The subject is the good, pious man.</meta>
for he shines forth in piety, religion, prudence, worship and veneration of God, having beheld true reason as if with his eyes; and by the confidence of his belief he excels among men as far as the sun surpasses the other stars with its light. For the sun itself lights up the other stars not so much by the greatness of its power as by its divinity and holiness. For believe, O Asclepius, that this is a second god <note>original: "Secundum deum"; the Hermetic texts often call the sun a visible "second god," an image of the invisible supreme God</note>, governing all other things and illuminating all the living beings of the world, whether animate or inanimate. For if the world is a living being, always living, which was, and is, and will be, nothing in the world is mortal. For in each living part that is in the world itself, as in one and the same ever-living creature, there is no place for mortality. Therefore God himself must be completely full of life and eternity, if he must necessarily live forever. So the sun, just as the world is everlasting, is likewise forever the governor of living things, the one who constantly attends to their whole vitality and dispenses it. <note>original: "frequentator, & dispensator"; the sun is pictured as a steward who keeps visiting and distributing life</note> God, therefore, is the everlasting governor of living and life-bearing things that are in the world, and the eternal dispenser of that life. Yet he dispensed it once and for all by an eternal law, granting life to all living things, in the manner that I shall now describe.

<summary>Hermes compares the pious man, who outshines other people, to the sun, which outshines the stars by its holiness. The sun is presented as a "second god" governing and distributing life to an ever-living world in which nothing truly dies, under an eternal law set by God.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, Asclepius, sun, second god, piety, living world, world soul, immortality, eternity, governor of life, eternal law, Hermeticism</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: Chapter 24, on musical harmony and its powers. The opening refers to the floating islands of a lake that move to music.</meta>

proceeding from the mainland into the lake, moving in a circle, they lead a dance, and then return to the shores. Marcus Varro testifies that he saw them. <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116 to 27 BC), the Roman scholar; the story of the dancing islands of Lydia is reported by Pliny the Elder.</note> And there are things more wondrous than these: for on the Attic shore the sea sounds like a lyre. <note>original: "citharam sonat"; the cithara was the concert lyre of the ancient Greeks.</note> At Megara a certain stone plays like a lyre at every stroke; so great is the power of Music. <note>Pausanias describes a stone at Megara that rang like a lyre string when struck; legend said Apollo had laid his lyre upon it.</note> Music itself soothes the soul, lifts up the mind, rouses warriors to battle, and eases the labors and weariness of every kind of work. It calls back the fallen and the despairing, and it comforts travelers. And the Arabs say that camels carrying loads are strengthened when their drivers sing. In the same way, those who carry heavy loads sing, and are made more able and lightened by it: for song produces delight and readiness. It calms the wrathful, gladdens the sad and anxious, makes peace among those in discord, tempers the rage of the frenzied, and scatters vain thoughts. Hence it is that Democritus and Theophrastus affirm that certain diseases of the body and of the mind can in this way be either cured or brought on. <note>Democritus, the Greek atomist philosopher, and Theophrastus, Aristotle's successor, were both cited in antiquity for the healing power of music; Theophrastus reportedly held that the flute could ease sciatica.</note> Thus we read that Terpander and Arion of Methymna <note>Terpander, a seventh-century BC poet-musician of Lesbos, and Arion of Methymna, the legendary singer said to have been saved from drowning by a dolphin.</note>

<summary>Agrippa continues his chapter on the powers of music with marvels from ancient authors: dancing islands, a sea that sounds like a lyre, and a ringing stone at Megara. He lists music's effects on the emotions and on work, including Arab camel drivers singing to their animals, and notes the ancient belief that music can cure or cause illness.</summary>
<keywords>Agrippa, Occult Philosophy, music, harmony, Marcus Varro, Megara, Attica, Arabs, camels, Democritus, Theophrastus, Terpander, Arion of Methymna, music therapy, emotions</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: "For Envy has departed from us;"</meta>
for the good of truth is inborn, together with life and light; and no avenger of wrath came near any longer. <note>original: "nec ultra ire uindex accessit"; "ire" is read here as "iræ," "of wrath." The "avengers" are the twelve tormenting vices of the body.</note> Rather, all the avengers were driven out by a sudden onrush. You have understood, my son, the manner of rebirth itself: when the number ten is present, the intellectual generation is composed, and it casts out the number twelve. <note>The ten divine powers, introduced on the previous page, replace the twelve vices; the "intellectual generation" is the spiritual birth of the mind.</note> And this we have beheld from the generation itself. Whoever, therefore, through the kindness of the generation that is according to God, lets go of bodily sense, knows himself to be composed of divine things; and having become unswerving, he rejoices with his whole mind in divine power. **TATIUS.** O father, I conceive it, not by the sight of the eyes but by the activity of the mind, which works through the inmost powers. I am in heaven, in earth, in water, in air. I am in animals, in trees; in the body, before the body, and after the body. <note>Tat describes the mystical experience of rebirth: the reborn mind feels itself present in all things and in all times.</note> But tell me this as well: how are the avenging darknesses, twelve in number, driven back by the ten powers? What is the manner of it, Trismegistus? **TRISMEGISTUS.** This tabernacle, O son, is built from the zodiac circle, which consists of that number twelve. <note>The "tabernacle" or tent is the human body, shaped by the twelve signs of the zodiac, which give rise to the twelve vices.</note> And its numbers are eleven, yet one and all-formed according to the ideas of nature, for the wandering and circuit of man. <note>original: "Numeriq; undecim sunt: unus omniformisq;"; the Latin is obscure here and may reflect a faulty reading. The sense seems to be that the twelve, though many, form a single nature taking every shape, which leads man astray.</note> Thus those avengers are in some way separated from one another, yet in acting they are in some way joined together: see how recklessness cannot be separated from anger. Rightly, therefore, according to right reason, they withdraw only so far as they are driven back by the ten powers, that is, by the number ten. The number ten, O son, is the begetter of the soul. But life

<summary>Hermes explains to his son Tat that the ten divine powers, the number of the soul, expel the twelve vices born of the zodiac, completing spiritual rebirth. Tat, now reborn, declares that he perceives himself present in all things, in heaven, earth, and every living being.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, Tat, Corpus Hermeticum, rebirth, regeneration, number ten, number twelve, zodiac, vices, divine powers, avengers, mystical experience, Marsilio Ficino</keywords>

and will mingle itself with the waters of its own fountain. Therefore the gods are the rulers of all species; these are followed by gods whose ruler is <term>ousia</term> <gloss>essence, being</gloss>. These are the sensible gods, alike to both their origins, who make all things through sensible nature, each one illuminating his own work, one through another. Of heaven, or whatever is contained under that name, the <term>ousiarch</term> <gloss>ruler of essence</gloss> is Jupiter. For through heaven Jupiter gives life to all things. Of the sun the ousiarch is light. For the good of light is poured into us through the orb of the sun. Of the thirty-six (whose name is Horoscopes) <note>The thirty-six "decans," star groups each governing ten degrees of the zodiac in Egyptian astrology.</note> among the stars that are always fixed in the same place, the ousiarch or ruler is the one they call Pantomorphos, or Omniform, who makes different forms in different species. The seven spheres that are called wandering <note>The seven planets known to antiquity, including the sun and moon.</note> have their ousiarchs, that is, their rulers, which they call Fortune and <term>Heimarmene</term> <gloss>Fate</gloss>, by which all things are changed, through the law of nature, with the firmest stability, and varied by everlasting motion. The air, however, is the instrument or machine of all things, through which all things come to be. Its ousiarch is the second <note>The text appears to break off here; most editions mark a gap at this point.</note> mortal things to mortals, and things like these. These things, then, being so, moving from the lowest to the highest, all things are so linked together, belonging to one another by nature, that mortal things are bound to mortal, and sensible things to sensible; but the summit of government obeys that highest Lord, so that they are not many, but rather one. For all things hang from one, or rather flow down from it; when they are seen as apart, they are believed to be many and separate, but united they are one, or rather two: that from which all things come to be, and that by which they come to be. That is, the matter from which they are made, and the will of him at whose nod the rest are brought about. **ASCLEPIUS.** What is this reasoning again, O Trismegistus? **TRISMEGISTUS.** It is this, O Asclepius. For God, or the Father, or the Lord

<margin><unclear>Right margin cut off: only fragments of a marginal commentary survive, "nu / cti / ct / ni / cup / nu: / qu / to / cit / riu / oin / eni / pa / no / ni / on / bus / xus / pre / tas / rer / nia / nat / clep / vtri / gu / ma / qu / eni / sem / sum / & n"</unclear></margin>

<summary>In this passage of the Asclepius, Hermes describes the hierarchy of gods and their "ousiarchs," or rulers of essence: Jupiter rules heaven, light rules the sun, Pantomorphos rules the thirty-six decans, and Fortune and Fate rule the seven planets. He concludes that all things, linked from lowest to highest, depend on one supreme Lord and are ultimately one, or rather two: matter and the divine will.</summary>

28 AURORA

<meta>continues from previous page: the opening words "se tulit" close the sentence about the sophistic whitening of copper with arsenic</meta>came to. For indeed, arsenic can scarcely be fixed at all <note>to "fix" a substance is to make it stable in the fire, so that it no longer flies off as vapor</note> unless the working artist has an equally thorough knowledge of its tinging spirit <note>original: "spiritum eius tingentem"; the active coloring principle of the substance</note>. On this very point all the philosophers have dozed, trying in vain to make something of it. Whoever, therefore, does not know this spirit should hold no hope of fixing arsenic, nor of giving it the power by which it may gain the perfection of transmutation. For this reason I make it known to all that the whitening mentioned above is drawn from a false foundation, and that by it copper is falsely whitened, not changed. The Sophists <note>Paracelsus's name for fraudulent or misguided alchemists who imitated the outward signs of the Art</note> mixed <term>Venus</term> <gloss>copper</gloss>, masked and painted up in this way, with twice its weight of <term>Luna</term> <gloss>silver</gloss>, and sold it to goldsmiths and to mint-masters. In the end, however, they turned themselves into counterfeiters: not only those who sold it, but also those who bought it.

Some of the Sophists took red arsenic <note>probably realgar or orpiment, red and yellow arsenic sulfides</note> in place of white, and this too ended in a false art. For however it is prepared, it yields nothing but whiteness. Some went further still, to common sulphur, which, yellow as it is, they boiled in vinegar, lye, or very sharp urines for a day and a night, until it came out white. Afterwards they raised it from common salt and from lime of eggshells <note>original: "calce ouorum"; calcined eggshell, used as an alkaline base</note>, boiled it and sublimed it <note>sublimation: heating a solid so that it rises as vapor and settles again as a purified deposit</note> by sublimation, and this many times over. Yet it always remained combustible, though white. With it, however, to fix raw mercury

<summary>Paracelsus explains that arsenic cannot be fixed without knowing its "tinging spirit," and denounces the Sophists who whitened copper to pass it off as silver, becoming counterfeiters. He then lists further failed attempts using red arsenic and whitened, sublimed common sulphur.</summary>
<keywords>Paracelsus, Aurora, arsenic, fixation, tinging spirit, Sophists, counterfeiting, copper, Venus, silver, Luna, whitening, red arsenic, sulphur, sublimation, mercury, transmutation</keywords>

# FOURTH

<meta>continues from previous page: the sentence on the citrination of silver by sulphur; page 75, signature L iij</meta>is anything but brilliant; it is rather dusky and livid with a deadly earthiness. <term>Luna</term> <gloss>silver</gloss> is likewise turned yellow with a solution of <term>Mars</term> <gloss>iron</gloss>.

The method of that citrination <note>citrination: the yellowing of silver toward the color of gold</note> which is accomplished through <term>Vitriol</term> <gloss>a metallic sulfate</gloss> or <term>Copperas</term> <gloss>green vitriol, iron sulfate</gloss> is as follows. Take a definite quantity of each of them, and sublime that part of it which allows itself to be sublimed, until it is sublimed entirely, with full driving-off. After this, sublime again what has been sublimed, with the degree of fire proper to it, so that some part of it is fixed after another, until the greater part of it is fixed. Afterwards treat it with careful attention to the fire, so that a greater fire may be applied to it to bring it to perfection. After this, let it be dissolved into a most deeply red water, which has no equal. From there you must use your ingenuity to give it entry into the body of <term>Luna</term> <gloss>silver</gloss>; and these devices have been shown to you sufficiently, if you are a diligent searcher of the complete work which we have written.

And because we see that these substances cling in friendly fashion to the depths of silver, we have therefore concluded, and it is certain, that they come from its root, and that is why silver happens to be altered by them. These, then, are all the medicines of the first order that we have set forth. Yet their methods can be multiplied in many ways, provided the essence of the coloring substances <note>original: "pigmentalium rerum"</note> is preserved through the variety of methods.

Some, indeed, have devised more medicines; but one of two things must necessarily follow. Either they must create their medicine from these same substances, or from things having the same nature. Or else they compose a medicine which, with its alteration, is equal to what does not exist, and which benefits neither the world nor the parts of the world, until the mover in the lofty movable of nature has come to rest uncorrupted. <note>An obscure closing phrase. It seems to mean that such invented medicines will never be of any use, as if "until the end of the world," when the heavenly mover of nature ceases its motion.</note>

<summary>The author completes his account of yellowing silver, adding a method with iron and a step-by-step procedure using vitriol or copperas: repeated sublimation, gradual fixation, and dissolution into a deep red water that can enter silver. He closes the medicines of the first order, noting that methods may vary but that newly invented medicines either rely on the same substances or are useless.</summary>
<keywords>Pseudo-Geber, Sum of Perfection, citrination, silver, Luna, iron, Mars, vitriol, copperas, sublimation, fixation, red water, medicines of the first order, alchemy</keywords>

THE CAUTERY. 381

<margin>15.</margin>
Pus, therefore, is blood corrupted in the part where the wound is, and the effect of a digestion corrupted in that same place. To have damaged the integrity, continuity and digestion of the parts, and finally to have turned blood into pus: this very thing is reckoned in the *Schools* <note>the university medicine of the Galenic tradition, which Van Helmont attacks throughout</note> as having headed off *Catarrhs* <note>catarrh: a supposed downflow of waste fluid from the head to other parts of the body</note>. Either it has drawn out through the hole of the cautery an excremental humor from the head (from which they derive all *Catarrhs* in the first place), a humor which otherwise threatened to settle upon a <term>noble part</term> <gloss>a vital organ</gloss>; or else, meanwhile, there is a sympathy between the head and the wounded part, or there is not. It is all the same to them, so long as the skin is kept wounded. Whether that excremental humor is blood, or becomes pus or <term>sanies</term> <gloss>a thin, bloody discharge</gloss>, it is all the same, so long as the world is taken in by the worn-out words catarrh, precaution, derivation, revulsion <note>derivation and revulsion: Galenic terms for drawing a humor away to a nearby part or to a distant part</note>, and <term>fontanelle</term> <gloss>an artificial ulcer kept open to drain humors</gloss>.

For I look upon an infant of this year, already teething, suffering fever, foam at the mouth, and ceaseless drooling; and at length gripes come, and stools of greenish yellow. Well, that tooth is part of the head: therefore the diarrhea will be a Catarrh of the head! But what sympathy has a tooth about to break through, or a swollen gum, with the intestine? Or what power has it to generate and send a Catarrh from the little infant's stomach to the head, and from there into the *Ileum* <note>the lower part of the small intestine</note>? By what right will a vapor distilled from the stomach become verdigris-green bile in the head? Has the workshop of bile, perhaps, already moved to the head at the very start of life? Could a cautery (if the infant could bear it) draw the leek-green diarrhea into itself, and make up for several pounds of leek-green bile with a few little drops of pus? Why does the infant's stomach fabricate a Catarrh because of the pain of a tooth? Why is it sent into the Intestine, and not to the aching tooth? Does the reader not yet see that diarrhea is not a Catarrh? Rather, the angered *Archeus* <note>Van Helmont's term, taken from Paracelsus, for the vital governing spirit that directs each bodily process</note>, anywhere it may be, stands ready in the Intestine to change the nourishing cream <note>original: "alimentarium cremorem"; the chyle, the milky product of digestion</note> into excrements, which the *Schools* take to be bile, phlegm, and so forth. If, then, diarrhea is not a Catarrh, and the angered

<column-break/>

*Archeus* can change anything into a hostile liquid merely because the gum is afflicted, will it not be able to unload itself in any direction through the established outlets <note>original: "emunctoria"; the natural channels of excretion</note>? Will it not do so without waiting for a skin opened by a caustic? Ah, has a cruel dullness made the *Schools* rage against mortals of their own kind?
<margin>16.</margin>
For they do not consider that in women and in fat people the fleshy membrane around the usual sites of a cautery is mere grease, at least two fingers thick; and yet these are the very persons to whom cauteries are urged most often, and as most beneficial. Hence the bottom of the fontanelle will scarcely reach halfway through the fat.
<margin>17.</margin>
There is therefore no way by which the wicked, fictitious humor of *Catarrh*, banished from the brain or from between the skull and the skin, could rush down through the middle of the fat. But what, after all, is that solitary humor which, banished for its own sin by the part that sends it, descends unmixed through the substance of the fat and degenerates into pus? If it is an exhalation of vapors from the stomach, why will it not be more frequent in the young and in those with hot stomachs than in the weak, the old, and the cold? How will that water, distilled from vapor, take on the form of pus? How will it hurry through the brain, the <term>meninges</term> <gloss>the membranes around the brain</gloss>, and the skull to find the hole made by the cautery, so that it flows down and is purged only there? Why does the vapor not fly off into the air a hundred times before it reaches the place marked out for the cautery at the surgeon's pleasure? How will water climbing from the stomach now be blood, and the mother of pus? How will blood (the matter of pus, according to *Galen* <note>the Greek physician of the 2nd century AD whose teachings dominated the Schools</note>) be the matter of *Catarrh*? Why should blood be reduced to the rank of the bad humors, when, not yet contaminated, it is sent out by nature to the wounded place? Why, once the wound is made, will nature stop driving the condemned matter out through, and into, the places it is used to? When the skin is opened at the healer's whim, will nature forget all its other paths? Did it perhaps labor only to find an exit somewhere, and, that being done, will it from now on come obediently to the one who wounds? Therefore these four things are false,

<meta>signature D d d; the catchword "nempè" is not translated</meta>

<summary>Van Helmont argues that pus is simply blood spoiled at the site of the wound, and mocks the Schools' claim that cauteries drain a "catarrh" from the head. Using a teething infant with diarrhea and the thick fat of women and stout patients as examples, he shows that no humor could travel from the brain to the cautery, and that the Archeus can expel waste through the body's own outlets.</summary>
<keywords>Van Helmont, cautery, fontanelle, pus, blood, catarrh, Archeus, Schools, Galen, teething, infant diarrhea, bile, fat, humors, derivation, revulsion</keywords>

<margin>The Magnet of Man. A Magical cure, in which there is a celestial impression: after contact with the herb, the herb, until it has rotted, draws the medicine into the ulcer, and so heals it.</margin>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>manner, the greater part of the diseases that come from heavenly Influence, and from the Astral Impression of the Firmament of the Greater World <note>the macrocosm, the universe, as opposed to the Lesser World, the human body</note>, will not be cured by indiscriminate Remedies, such as the Arcana <note>secret remedies holding the concentrated virtue of a substance</note> of herbs, minerals, and metals. Instead, the cure should be undertaken through Astronomical Influence, at least with those things which have an Analogy to the greater and lesser world. In these lies the true Magnetic power of the Firmament and the Celestial Impression for resisting diseases from the Firmament of the greater and lesser world, as is seen in <term>Persicaria</term> <gloss>water-pepper</gloss>, the greater <term>Solidago</term> <gloss>goldenrod</gloss>, <term>Dracunculus</term> <gloss>dragonwort</gloss>, and the greater <term>Symphytum</term> <gloss>comfrey</gloss>.

If a disease or pain has been brought on Supernaturally, by incantation or by the Magical Impression of the Ascendants <note>the rising signs and influences of the heavens at a given moment</note>, then the attempt to heal by the former three is in vain. Rather, following Paracelsus, one must proceed Magically and Supernaturally, and the evil must be driven back in turn by the same means by which it was brought in. Otherwise, in the said Simples <note>single medicinal plants, used unmixed</note> there is an attractive power of Influence, and by Divine ordinance they all cure Magically, Astronomically, and Magnetically, because the medicine is in them, and the Magnet is in Man. For just as the Sun and the Stars have the power of drawing moisture from lower things, so Man (by his inborn magnetic power of attraction, like a Magnet drawing the spirit of iron in place of nourishment) and the Lower things have the same power of drawing from the Higher, as we see in time of Plague; and these draw

## DIALOGUE XXVI.

> Praise sparingly; for when you have praised unjustly,
> If you then condemn again, it will look like fickleness.

*Sorrow.* I am accused of having praised an unworthy man.

*Reason.* <meta>The OCR repeats Sorrow's line "Laudasse arguor indignum" at the start of Reason's reply; this appears to be a transcription duplication and is not rendered twice.</meta> It is indeed a fault, but it often grows from a good root. For good and innocent people imagine others to be such as they are themselves. This makes them readier to praise than is right. And although I admit that praising the unworthy is bad, blaming the undeserving is far worse.

*Sorrow.* I praised an unworthy man.

*Reason.* If you did it knowingly, you deserve blame; but if unknowingly, you can be excused. Even so, it is a lesser evil to be deceived than to deceive. For being deceived is another's crime; deceiving is the deceiver's own.

*Sorrow.* Another man's praise is turning into my disgrace.

But we shall easily be freed from such scruples if we turn our mind to that dispensation of God which I have noted: that he wished, for that time when he was handing down his Testament, still in some way wrapped up, to the Israelite people, to signify and figure both the grace of future and eternal happiness by earthly benefits, and the gravity of spiritual death by bodily punishments.

4 The second difference between the Old and New Testament is placed in figures: that the former, with the truth absent, displayed only an image, and a shadow in place of the body; the latter shows the truth present and the solid body. And this is mentioned almost wherever the new testament is set against the old; yet it is treated more fully in the Epistle to the Hebrews than anywhere else. There the Apostle argues against those who did not think the observances of the Mosaic Law could be abolished without dragging with them the ruin of the whole of religion. To refute this error, he takes up <margin>Psalm 110, b, 4</margin> what had been foretold by the Prophet about the priesthood of Christ. For since an eternal priesthood is conferred on him, it is certain that the priesthood in which successors were substituted for one another every day is abolished. And he proves that the institution of this new priest prevails because <margin>Hebrews 7, b, 11; c, 19; and 9, c, 9; and 10, a, 1</margin> it is established by an oath. He adds afterward that in this transfer of the priesthood a change of the Testament is also involved. And he confirms by reason that this was necessary, since such was the weakness of the Law that it could bring nothing to perfection. Then he goes on to explain what that weakness was: namely, that it had outward righteousnesses of the flesh, which could not make its worshippers perfect according to conscience; that by the sacrifices of beasts it could neither blot out sins nor procure true holiness. He concludes, therefore, that there was in it a shadow of good things to come, not the living image of the things themselves; and so it had no other office than to be an introduction into a better hope, which is shown forth in the Gospel.

Here we must see in what respect the covenant of the Law is compared with the covenant of the Gospel, and the ministry of Christ with that of Moses. For if the comparison concerned the substance of the promises, there would be a great disagreement between the two Testaments; but since the state of the question leads us elsewhere, we must aim there in order to find the truth. Let us, then, set in the middle the covenant which God once ratified as eternal and never to perish. Its fulfillment, from which it finally has its firmness and validity, is Christ. While such confirmation is awaited, the Lord prescribes ceremonies through Moses, which are like solemn symbols of that confirmation. What came into dispute was this: whether the ceremonies ordained in the Law ought to give way to Christ. These, although they were only accidents of the covenant, or certainly additions and appendages, and (as the common people say) <term>accessoria</term> <gloss>accessories</gloss>, yet because they were the instruments for administering it, they bear the name of covenant; as is also customarily given to other Sacraments. In sum, therefore, the Old Testament is here called the solemn manner of confirming the covenant, comprised in ceremonies and sacrifices. Since nothing solid lies beneath it unless one passes further, the Apostle contends that it had to be made obsolete and abrogated, so that place might be given to Christ, the guarantor and mediator of a better Testament, through whom eternal sanctification has been acquired once for all for the elect, and the transgressions which remained under the Law have been blotted out.

Or, if you prefer, take it this way: the old Testament of the Lord was that which was handed down wrapped in the shadowy and ineffectual observance of ceremonies; and it was therefore temporary, because it was, as it were, held in suspense until it should rest on a firm and substantial confirmation. Only then did it become new and eternal, after it had been consecrated and established by the blood of Christ. Hence Christ calls the cup which he offers to the disciples at the Supper <margin>Matthew 26, c, 28</margin> the cup of the New Testament in his blood: to signify that the Testament of God truly attains its truth at the moment when it is sealed with his blood, by which it becomes new and eternal.

5 From this it is clear in what sense the Apostle said that the Jews were led <margin>Galatians 3, d, 24; and 4, a, 1</margin> to Christ by the <term>paedagogia</term> <gloss>tutelage, the guardianship of a child's attendant</gloss> of the Law before he was shown forth in the flesh. He also confesses that they were sons and heirs of God, but such as had to be kept, because of their childhood, under the custody of a tutor. <note>In the ancient world a <term>paedagogus</term> was the slave who escorted and supervised a child, not a teacher in the modern sense.</note> For it was fitting, while the sun of righteousness had not yet risen, that there should be neither so great a brightness of revelation nor so great a sharpness of understanding. So the Lord dispensed the light of his word to them in such a way that they still saw it from afar and dimly. Therefore Paul marks this slenderness of understanding with the word "childhood": the Lord willed it to be exercised in the elements of this world and in petty outward observances, as in the rules of a child's discipline, until Christ should shine forth, through whom the knowledge of the faithful people was to grow to maturity.
